scenes.heading: Angle chasing
scenes.sub: Follow the clues to the hidden angle
scenes.say: Some angles are hidden deep inside a diagram. You cannot find them in one step, but you can chase them, one rule at a time.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A treasure hunt: each clue leads to the next clue
scenes.science: Each angle rule leads you to the next angle
scenes.breaks: a treasure hunt has one path, but an angle chase often has several routes, and you may draw your own extra lines.
scenes.say: Think of a treasure hunt. The first clue does not show you the treasure. It sends you to the next clue. In angle chasing, the angle you are given is the first clue, and each rule moves you to a new angle. Unlike a treasure hunt, there are often several routes, and you are allowed to draw extra lines.

scenes.heading: Your toolkit
points: F and Z equal, C adds to 180°
Exterior angle = sum of two opposite inside
scenes.say: Every step uses one rule from your toolkit. Straight lines and points. Vertically opposite angles. The F, Z and C rules for parallel lines. The triangle sum, equal base angles in an isosceles triangle, and the exterior angle rule. Write the reason after every step.

scenes.heading: Ticks mean equal sides and equal angles
notes: AB = AC, so base angles are equal
scenes.say: First the triangle, then the tick marks on two sides. Equal sides mean an isosceles triangle, so the two base angles are equal. With a forty degree apex, the base angles share one hundred and forty degrees, so each one is seventy.
scenes.caption: Equal sides mean an isosceles triangle, so the two base angles are equal. With a 40° apex, the base angles share 140°, so each one is 70°.

scenes.heading: The bent line: add the two angles
notes: Draw a dashed line through the bend
Two Z shapes: the bend = p + q
scenes.say: Here a line bends between two parallel lines. No rule connects the angles yet, so draw a dashed line through the bend, parallel to the others. Now you can see two Z shapes. The top part of the bend equals p and the bottom part equals q, so the bend angle is p plus q.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: AB = AC and ∠BAC = 52°. BC is extended to D. Find ∠ACD.
scenes.say: The triangle is isosceles, so the base angles share one hundred and eighty minus fifty-two, which is one hundred and twenty-eight. Each base angle is sixty-four degrees. Then angles on a straight line: one hundred and eighty minus sixty-four gives one hundred and sixteen degrees.
scenes.caption: The base angles share 180 − 52 = 128°, so each is 64°. Angles on a straight line: 180 − 64 = 116°.

scenes.heading: Angles with algebra
scenes.question: ∠A = x°, ∠B = 2x°, and the exterior angle at C is 132°. Find x.
scenes.say: The exterior angle equals the two interior opposite angles added together. So x plus two x equals one hundred and thirty-two. Three x equals one hundred and thirty-two, so x is forty-four.
scenes.caption: The exterior angle equals the two interior opposite angles added: x + 2x = 132, so 3x = 132 and x = 44.

points: One rule and one reason per step
Ticks: equal sides, equal base angles
scenes.say: Quick recap. Chase one step at a time and give a reason for each. Ticks mean equal base angles. An exterior angle equals the two opposite angles inside. And if you get stuck, draw a construction line. Now try the practice questions!
